title: Industry II: Five Forces — Where the Profit Goes
keyQuestion: How did Coke structure an industry to give itself a competitive advantage?

reading.name: Where the Profit Goes (Five Forces Brief)

case.name: The US Carbonated Drink Wars in 2026 (Cola Wars Case 2026)

slides: No slides for this session (Canvas). PROVA Case Quiz 1: evaluate the cola CONCENTRATE industry with Five Forces.

framework.name: Porter's Five Forces
framework.summary: Before 'how do we win?' ask 'is this game worth winning?' Structure sets a ceiling on returns that varies roughly seven-fold across industries. Five parties contend for the value an industry creates; suppliers, buyers, entrants and substitutes take their share, and what remains is what rivals compete over. Industry profitability is the residual.

components.name: Threat of new entrants
components.what: Not whether anyone entered, but what a determined, well-capitalized entrant would face: scale economies, capital requirements, switching costs, control of distribution, regulation, incumbency advantages money can't buy quickly (data, decades-old brand, installed base) — plus expected retaliation. Most dangerous when latent: 'High returns in an accessible industry are a countdown, not an achievement.'

components.name: Supplier power
components.what: Strong when suppliers are more concentrated than the industry, the input is differentiated or has high switching costs, the industry is a minor customer, no substitute exists, or forward integration is credible. Labor is a supplier. Test: for every input that matters, how many qualified alternatives exist and what would it cost to qualify another?

components.name: Buyer power
components.what: Strong when buyers are few or buy in volume, the product is undifferentiated, switching costs are low, the purchase is a large share of the buyer's costs, or backward integration is credible. Distribution channels hold buyer power independent of end customers. Power is only partly about size.

components.name: Threat of substitutes
components.what: Performs the same function by different means, so it doesn't appear in the industry's competitive set (video calls vs. business travel; index funds vs. active; lab-grown vs. mined). Places a ceiling on price industry discipline cannot lift; wins on a trajectory, so incumbents misjudge timing.

components.name: Rivalry
components.what: Most destructive with many similar competitors, slow growth, high fixed/low marginal cost, large capacity increments, commodity products, high exit barriers. The DIMENSION matters as much as intensity: price rivalry transfers value to customers; rivalry on features, brand, service can expand value.

components.name: Structure vs. position (capital allocation)
components.what: Two axes: attractiveness of structure × strength of position. Attractive/strong: invest and defend. Attractive/weak: harvest or exit (fix fast or sell). Unattractive/strong: milk, or reshape (most commonly misread — cash reinvested into the same structure). Unattractive/weak: exit (the most expensive quadrant, where effort feels virtuous and returns nothing).

components.name: Three uses: position, exploit change, reshape
components.what: Position where forces are weakest (segments differ); exploit change in the forces before rivals; reshape the structure (consolidation, switching costs, standards, supplier development, demand creation) — the highest-return move. Name in advance which force an initiative changes and by what mechanism; otherwise it is an operating improvement.

components.name: Government and complements
components.what: Not a sixth force (Porter 2008): both operate THROUGH the five. Regulation raising entry costs strengthens barriers; interoperability mandates strengthen buyers; a complement controlled by one powerful party behaves like a powerful supplier.

terms.def: The configuration of the five forces that sets the ceiling on returns available to any competitor in the industry.
Porter's 1992-2006 US ROIC data: average 14.9%; security brokers 40.9%, soft drinks and prepackaged software 37.6%, pharma 31.7%, airlines 5.9% — roughly seven to one, persistent for decades.
What remains after suppliers (input cost), buyers (price pressure), entrants (added capacity) and substitutes (price ceiling) take their share.
Entry that hasn't happened yet but caps returns at the level that would attract it.
Entrants model the incumbent's response; a credible history of defense deters entry the arithmetic alone would encourage.
One of the one or two forces that account for most of an industry's structural effect; identifying them is the objective of the analysis.
The cola industry's vertical split: capital-light, brand-driven, ~31% EBITDA concentrate vs. capital-intensive, 5-10% operating margin bottling.
Coke and Pepsi sell finished-goods rights to a few large bottlers while keeping national accounts, marketing and product development.

claims.claim: A competent management team in a structurally poor industry will usually underperform a mediocre one in a structurally good industry; no operating discipline closes that gap.
Five Forces is a theory of how the value an industry creates gets divided, not a market survey or list of events.
A profitable product line with a single qualified supplier is not as profitable as it looks: the supplier holds an option on the margin.

Proposition 1: structure sets the ceiling on returns, the ceiling varies by roughly a factor of seven, and no operating program lifts it; the decision to compete in an industry is larger than any decision made within it.
Proposition 2: the framework earns its keep used comparatively and converted into a decision: name the one or two binding forces, state which way they're moving, specify what would have to change.

Proposition 3: structure can be shaped, and the returns to shaping it exceed the returns to performing well within it; know which conditions were built rather than found, because anything built can be dismantled.
A business generating strong cash in a structurally deteriorating industry is a source of funds, not a use; the burden of proof on reinvestment should be high.

The diamond industry manufactured both scarcity and the social norm that supported its prices — the most complete example of structural engineering, and a reminder a manufactured structure can be dismantled.

failures.name: Defining the industry incorrectly
failures.what: The most common and consequential error. Too broad averages away different structures; too narrow excludes substitutes and entrants by definition. Test: do firms inside the boundary face the same forces and readily serve each other's customers? Boundaries are geographic too.

failures.name: Mistaking growth for attractiveness
failures.what: Growth is not a force; it often attracts entry and capacity faster than demand (airlines, solar modules, food delivery, streaming). Ask what growth does to each force.

failures.name: Confusing your position with the industry's structure
failures.what: A strong competitor in a poor industry concludes the industry is fine. Structure = what returns are available; position = what share you capture.

failures.name: Treating the analysis as a snapshot
failures.what: Run it at two points in time; a force weak today and strengthening is the one to act on.

failures.name: Adding a sixth box
failures.what: Resist adding government or complements; identify which of the five a factor operates through. That answer is actionable; a sixth box is not.

caseFacts.fact: Concentrate per-case economics (2025): sales $1.30, COGS $0.30 (23.1%), gross profit $1.00 (76.9%), advertising $0.28 (21.5%), G&A $0.32 (24.6%), EBITDA $0.40 (30.8%).
caseFacts.why: The 'extraordinarily profitable' half of the chain; contrast with bottling at 5-10% operating margins, ROIC often below the cost of capital.

caseFacts.fact: A concentrate plant for 10% of the market costs $35-70M (<1% of a year's concentrate sales at 10% share); a bottling plant costs $300-750M for 250-500M cases; ~3 plants for 10% share = $1,575M; total entry ~$1,628M if a niche entrant can't access refranchised networks.
caseFacts.why: The entry barrier isn't the concentrate plant — it's access to bottling/distribution (which Coke and Pepsi control).

caseFacts.fact: Shares 2025: Coca-Cola 46%, PepsiCo 25%, KDP 22%, private label ~3%, all others ~4% (functional soda ~1-1.5% of volume). Big three ~90%+ of volume.
caseFacts.why: Concentrated rivalry; C4 ≈ 96 (three firms + private label). Rivalry has historically been on advertising/brand, not price.

caseFacts.fact: Coke raised US concentrate prices 5-7% a year 2021-2024 with volume declines under 1% a year.
caseFacts.why: Pricing power evidence: buyers (bottlers, retailers) and substitutes did not cap price — yet.

caseFacts.fact: Exclusive bottler territories and 10-20 year fountain exclusives (McDonald's/BK/Wendy's = Coke; Yum!/Subway = Pepsi); PepsiCo bought Pizza Hut (1977), Taco Bell (1978), KFC (1986) partly to secure fountain sales. A 20-oz cold bottle returns 5-7x the per-ounce margin of a supermarket 12-pack.
caseFacts.why: How the concentrate producers structured the chain: control distribution and channels, keep the high-margin layer, push capital intensity onto bottlers.

caseFacts.fact: Per-capita CSD consumption fell from 53 gallons (1998 peak) to 28 (2025); dollar sales still grew 2-4% a year on mix and price.
caseFacts.why: Direction of the substitute force: water ($36B→$58B), energy ($12B→$24B), RTD coffee/tea, and functional soda (<$0.1B → $1.2B, 50%+ growth) are all moving against CSDs.

caseFacts.fact: PepsiCo bought poppi for $1.95B (~20x revenue) in 2025 after its internal SoulBoost failed; Coke discussed acquisitions; PepsiCo paid $550M for 8.5% of Celsius and distribution rights.
caseFacts.why: Incumbents responding to entry via niches by buying rather than building (links to Cracking Markets §7).

caseFacts.fact: Regulatory front: SNAP waivers restricting soda (Nebraska May 2025; 18 states ~28% of SNAP recipients by Q1 2026; 1.5-3% volume hit in affected states), front-of-pack warnings, dye phase-outs, municipal sugar taxes; Mexico's 2014 tax cut consumption 7.6% in year one.
caseFacts.why: Government operating THROUGH the forces: lowers demand and strengthens substitutes rather than acting as a sixth force.

caseFacts.fact: Dr Pepper became the #2 single brand (tied in 2023 at 8.34% vs. Pepsi 8.31%; clear #2 by 2024) partly by riding Coke and Pepsi bottlers who carry it because it isn't a cola.
caseFacts.why: Shows the distribution system as the moat and how a non-cola can use incumbents' networks.

strongAnalysis: Define the industry correctly first: concentrate production (US), not 'beverages' and not bottling — they face very different forces (PROVA Quiz 1 asked about concentrate).

Concentrate THEN: entry low threat (barrier is bottling/distribution access and brand, plus retaliation), suppliers weak (commodity inputs: sweetener, caramel, packaging), buyers (bottlers) weak because Coke/Pepsi granted exclusive territories and controlled them, substitutes weak-to-moderate, rivalry intense but on advertising not price → very high returns (soft drinks 37.6% ROIC).

How Coke structured it: kept the capital-light, brand-heavy layer; pushed capital intensity to bottlers; used exclusive territories and refranchising to control the buyer force; locked fountain channels with long exclusives; competed with Pepsi on brand rather than price; built distribution density no entrant could replicate.

Concentrate NOW (direction): substitutes strengthening fast (water, energy, functional soda), regulators/government acting through demand and substitutes, consumer shift; entry via niches (poppi/Olipop) succeeding because they avoid incumbents' channels; buyer power of retailers rising in take-home. Binding forces: substitutes and (through them) rivalry for the consumer occasion.

Capital allocation: strong position in a deteriorating structure → 'milk, or reshape' — use CSD cash to reshape (functional and energy portfolios) rather than reinvest into the same structure (5F Fig.3).

counter.argument: Coke's advantage is its brand, not industry structure — the brand would earn premium margins in any structure (a VRIO resource), so Five Forces overstates the role of structure.
counter.response: Both are true and they answer different questions (structure vs. position, 5F §4). Five Forces explains why the whole concentrate layer (including Pepsi and KDP) earns ~30% while bottling earns 5-10% — the same brands, different structure. Coke's brand explains its share of the concentrate pool. And the brand's value depends on structural choices: exclusive bottlers and channel control are what keep buyers weak and entrants out.

courseMap.text: Where profit lives: Five Forces sets the ceiling; PEST (S3) tells you which forces are about to move; concentration (S5) measures one input to rivalry; generic strategies (S1) are the firm's answer to the forces; VRIO (S6) explains position within the structure.
